blurb: The repos and skills from the 22 October issue, with what each one does and the setup steps from its own README.
intro: Issue #24 had six repos and three AI skills, and this page covers eight of them. There's a mix here: two desktop apps anyone can install, a CSS file for people who make web pages, and server tools for developers. If you only try one, make it DigUp, which searches your own files by what's in them. If you use a coding agent, map-design is the quickest skill to get something out of.

items.name: Strata
items.cost: Free (MIT). No account and no cloud
items.works_with: Windows, Linux and macOS. Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode and other apps that speak the OpenAI or Anthropic API
items.short: Runs Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, a 125B model that normally needs a server, on a gaming PC and serves it to your apps on localhost.
items.what: Strata makes a 125-billion-parameter model fit on a normal PC by splitting it across your graphics card, your RAM and your SSD. It chats, writes code and reads pictures. It serves the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs on `127.0.0.1:8080`, so coding agents can use it in place of a cloud model. You can run it as a desktop app or as the `strata` command in a terminal.
items.who: People with a gaming PC or Apple Silicon Mac who want a strong model running locally, with their chats and files staying on their own machine. Skip it if you have less than 32 GB of RAM and graphics memory together, or no room for a download of 40 to 70 GB.
needs: At least 32 GB of RAM and graphics memory (VRAM) together. 64 GB of RAM runs every size
An NVIDIA RTX 20 series or newer, an AMD Radeon RX 6800 or newer, Intel Arc, or an Apple Silicon Mac on macOS 15 or newer
About 80 GB of free disk. An SSD makes the first start much faster
Windows 10 or 11, Linux or macOS, with a current graphics driver
On Linux, FUSE 2 for the AppImage (`libfuse2` or `libfuse2t64`)

steps.title: Install the app
steps.text: Download the file for your system and graphics card from the releases page. For NVIDIA, take `cuda13` if your driver is 580 or newer, otherwise `cuda12`. The `hip` and `amd` files are for AMD cards. On Windows run the `.exe`, on Linux `chmod +x` the AppImage and start it, on a Mac drag Strata to Applications.

steps.title: Pick a model
steps.text: On the first screen the app reads your PC and recommends a model that fits. Press install. The download continues where it stopped if it is interrupted.

steps.title: Or install the terminal version (Linux and Mac)
steps.text: This pipes a script into your shell. The README shows how to download it with `-o install.sh` and read it first.

steps.title: Or install the terminal version (Windows PowerShell)
steps.text: Open a new terminal window afterwards.

steps.title: Start serving
steps.text: It asks one question at a time: model, context, pictures and who may connect. Then it downloads the engine and the model and starts serving.

steps.title: Connect your coding agent
steps.text: OpenAI-compatible apps use `http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1`. Anthropic API apps use `http://127.0.0.1:8080` without `/v1`. This command prints the exact settings for OpenCode, Codex CLI, Claude Code and others.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Set up Strata on this PC for me: https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata - follow docs/AI_SETUP.md in that repository.

watch: The one-line installers pipe a script straight into your shell. Read the script first.
The Windows installer is not code-signed yet, so Windows shows a "Windows protected your PC" warning.
The model is a big download: about 40 to 70 GB.
While the model starts, your PC can be slow or stop responding for 1 to 3 minutes. Strata loads 35 to 55 GB into RAM.
The app's chat can work in a folder on your PC. In Manual mode it asks before it changes a file or runs a command.
Web search in the chat is the one feature that sends something off your PC: the search words.
`strata launch --access lan` opens it to your phone or other PCs. It makes an API key by default, and `--no-api-key` turns that off.

items.name: SPACE
items.works_with: A Linux x86_64 host with KVM. Any app that can call an HTTP API
items.short: Perplexity's sandbox platform: your app creates isolated Firecracker microVMs over HTTP and runs agent or user code in them.
items.what: SPACE runs code in isolated Firecracker microVMs. Your application uses its HTTP API to create a Linux sandbox from a template, run commands in it, stream the output, and pause, suspend, wake or delete it. The local setup deploys it in a Kind (Kubernetes) cluster on your own machine.
items.who: Developers and platform teams who need a separate place to run code an agent or a user wrote. It is a server platform to deploy, so skip it if you want a sandbox you can use in a few minutes, or if you are on macOS.
needs: An apt-based Linux x86_64 host with KVM: `/dev/kvm`, `/dev/net/tun`, loop devices and btrfs support. A VM must support nested virtualization
A local Docker daemon that permits privileged containers
Bash, Git, curl, tar, OpenSSL, Python 3.8 or newer and `ssh-keygen`
Root or non-interactive sudo for the prerequisite installer

steps.title: Check the host and install tools
steps.text: The installation guide (`docs/installation.md`) has a block that checks the host, then one that runs `infra/space/kind/scripts/install-prereqs.sh`. That installs Kind, kubectl, Helm, grpcurl, Tilt, Go and jq into `$HOME/.local/bin`. Run each block in the same Bash session.

steps.title: Build and deploy
steps.text: The first build compiles the Rust workspace and builds the seed template. The `unset` lines stop bootstrap from copying cloud credentials into the cluster.
steps.code:
unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN
unset DD_API_KEY EPPO_SDK_KEY

export SPACE_VENDOR_ROOT="$HOME/.local/share/space/vendor"
export SPACE_KIND_CLUSTER=space-local

(
  set -euo pipefail

  time bash infra/space/kind/scripts/install-fc-vendor.sh
  time bash infra/space/kind/scripts/bootstrap.sh
)

steps.title: Verify and sign in
steps.text: Follow the guide's verify block, then its `authenticate` helper. It signs in as `root@local` and exports `SPACE_API_TOKEN`. The API is on port 8080 and the data plane on 8090.

steps.title: Run your first sandbox
steps.text: Run it from the repo root in the same shell. It creates a sandbox, runs a command, prints the output and asks whether to delete the sandbox.

steps.title: Remove it when you are done
steps.code:
SPACE_KIND_CLUSTER=space-local \
  bash infra/space/kind/scripts/teardown.sh &&
  unset SPACE_API_TOKEN &&
  kind get clusters

try.label: From the README
try.text: Run `python3 examples/first_sandbox.py`. You should see `Hello from SPACE` and `Command completed successfully`. Then edit its `COMMAND` constant to run your own command in the sandbox.

watch: The local deployment uses development passwords and signing keys. Keep it private and do not use production credentials.
The `root@local` password is `password` unless you set `SPACE_CONSOLE_PASSWORD` before bootstrap.
Bootstrap copies any AWS and Datadog credentials in your shell into cluster secrets, which is why the guide clears them first.
The prerequisite installer needs root or sudo and adds a PATH line to your Bash startup files.
It needs Docker to allow privileged containers. These steps do not run directly on macOS.
Fields marked `incubating` in the API schema are outside the supported contract.
Do not print or commit the API token.

items.name: DigUp
items.works_with: Apple Silicon Macs, Windows 10 and 11 (beta), Linux (beta)
items.short: Search the photos, PDFs, documents, recordings and videos on your computer by describing what is in them, all on-device.
items.what: DigUp indexes the folders you pick with Google DeepMind's EmbeddingGemma 2, which puts text, images, audio and video in one shared space. You press a shortcut, describe what you want, and it opens the PDF at the page or the video at the moment. Exact words like invoice numbers and error codes match too. Code search is there if you turn it on.
items.who: Anyone with a pile of files they can never find again, from screenshots to podcast recordings. Windows and Linux are still in beta and don't read the text inside screenshots yet.
needs: Mac: Apple Silicon with macOS 14 or later
Windows: 64-bit Windows 10 or 11
Linux: 64-bit Intel or AMD, Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12, Mint 21 or newer
About 865 MB for the model, downloaded once

steps.title: Install on a Mac
steps.text: Download the DMG from Releases and drag DigUp to Applications, or use Homebrew.

steps.title: Install on Windows
steps.text: Download `DigUp_x.y.z_x64-setup.exe` from the beta release and run it. It installs for you only, with no admin rights.

steps.title: Install on Linux
steps.text: On Ubuntu, Debian, Mint and similar, install the .deb. The package is called `dig-up`. Anywhere else, use the AppImage.

steps.title: Pick folders
steps.text: Open DigUp. While the model downloads, pick the folders to search. It shows how long the first pass will take for each one.

steps.title: Search
steps.text: Press ⇧⌘Space on a Mac or Ctrl+Shift+Space on Windows and Linux, in any app, and describe what you are looking for.

try.label: From the README
try.text: the clause about pets in the lease

watch: It goes online only to download the model once and to check for updates once a day. The update check sends nothing about your files, and you can turn it off.
The Windows installer isn't signed yet, so Windows may warn that it doesn't recognize the app.
The first pass can take an hour for a big Downloads folder on a Mac. On a processor alone, a large photo library can take hours.
It skips keys, certificates, password files and hidden folders like `.ssh`, and never changes, moves or uploads your files.
On a Mac, macOS asks once whether DigUp may control QuickTime Player to open videos at the right moment.

items.name: freehire
items.cost: Free (MIT). Some features need an LLM endpoint or draw on AI credits
items.works_with: Any browser at freehire.me. Self-hosting uses Docker Compose. There is a CLI and an MCP server for Claude Desktop and Claude Code
items.short: An open-source job search engine with over 3.3 million IT postings pulled straight from company career pages.
items.what: freehire crawls postings directly from companies' own applicant-tracking systems such as Workday, Greenhouse and Lever, collapses duplicates and links to the original posting. On top of the search it has a CV builder, an application tracker, an in-app agent and a keyless public API. You can use the hosted site or run the whole stack yourself.
items.who: Job seekers in IT can just use freehire.me. The repo is for developers who want to self-host it, build on the API or add a company's job board.
needs: Docker with Docker Compose, and `make`
Go, if you run the workers with `go run`
A `JWT_SECRET` in `.env` for local development. OAuth and LLM credentials are optional

steps.title: Use the hosted site
steps.text: If you just want to search jobs, go to freehire.me. The public API at `https://freehire.me/api/v1/jobs` needs no credential.

steps.title: Start the stack
steps.text: From the repo folder, this builds and starts the API, web app, Postgres, Meilisearch, Redis and S3 storage in Docker.

steps.title: Crawl some jobs
steps.text: Crawling and enrichment are run-once workers meant for cron. Each needs `DATABASE_URL`. This one crawls one provider's boards.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Narrow the live postings by region, work format, specialization and seniority, then follow a job straight to the company's own careers page.

watch: Features that need OAuth or LLM credentials stay disabled until you set them.
Some features draw on AI credits. The README points to `docs/features.md` for which ones.
The Chrome extension reads the page you're on when you ask it something and can fill in application forms for you.
Changing a migration does not re-apply to an existing database volume. The README's fix recreates the volume with `docker compose down -v && make up`.

items.name: Sumi.css
items.works_with: Any HTML page. Current Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari
items.short: A 6.7 KB CSS file that makes plain, semantic HTML look finished before you add a single class.
items.what: Sumi.css styles headings, forms, tables, cards, accordions, modals and navigation from the HTML elements alone. It follows the visitor's light or dark setting, and every color, font, size and radius is a CSS custom property. Element styles have zero specificity, so your own CSS wins without `!important`.
items.who: Anyone making a simple site, a prototype or docs page who wants it to look good without a build step or a big framework. If you already use a utility framework you like, you probably don't need it.
needs: An HTML page to style

steps.title: Link the file
steps.text: Copy `sumi.min.css` into your project and link it.

steps.title: Or load it from a CDN
Write plain HTML
steps.text: Use `<header>`, `<main>` and `<footer>` as direct children of `<body>` and they center themselves. Keep the viewport meta tag for phones and set `lang`. Add a class only when you want something specific, like `.grid` or `.callout`.

steps.title: Theme it
steps.text: Override the `--s-` custom properties in a stylesheet that loads after Sumi.

steps.title: Force a color mode
steps.text: Sumi follows the system setting by default.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Copy the README's quick start page into an HTML file next to `sumi.min.css` and open it. It is styled with almost no classes.

watch: It uses `:where()`, `:has()` and `color-mix()`, available from Chrome and Edge 111, Firefox 121 and Safari 16.2. Older browsers still show readable pages, with plainer hover and focus colors.
The CDN option loads the file from jsDelivr.
The dark palette appears twice in `sumi.css`. If you change dark colors, change both blocks.

items.name: qz-browser-agent
items.cost: Free (Apache 2.0). Model costs depend on your provider. Compatible local models are supported
items.works_with: Chrome and Edge. Claude Code, Codex, Grok Bot, pi and other agents that load AI skills
items.short: Lets your coding agent hand whole browser jobs, like cross-site research or data collection, to qz running in your own Chrome.
items.what: qz is a browser agent that runs as a Chrome extension in your own browser, with your logins and cookies. It researches across sites, collects data into tables or files and reports with sources. This skill teaches your coding agent to pair with qz through its CLI, give it a task, watch it, answer its questions and export the results.
items.who: People who already use a coding agent and want it to do web research or multi-step browsing that usually breaks on logins and long click paths. Skip it if you use Firefox, which qz doesn't support.
needs: Chrome or Edge with the qz extension
Node.js 22 or later
A model: an API key from a provider, a ChatGPT sign-in through OpenAI Codex, or a compatible local server
For account-specific work, be signed in to the target site in that Chrome profile

steps.title: Add the extension
steps.text: Click Add to Chrome on the Chrome Web Store, then click the qz icon to open the side panel. If you can't reach the store, the README explains how to load the release ZIP by hand.

steps.title: Connect a model
steps.text: Open Settings in qz, pick a provider, paste your API key and save.

steps.title: Pair once
steps.text: It pairs with your default browser.

steps.title: Ask your agent
steps.text: Tell your agent what you want and that it should use qz. qz works in the side panel, where you can watch every step and stop it.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Use qz to compare open-weight LLMs released in the last 6 months and put them in a table with sources.

watch: qz works in your real browser, on the sites you're already signed in to.
Your data goes to the model you configure and the websites qz visits. Task data is stored locally.
The skill tells the agent to ask you before purchases, posting, deletion or other changes you haven't authorized.
The CLI starts a local service and must run on the same machine as Chrome. A cloud shell can't reach your desktop browser.
`stop` disconnects every connected browser at once.

items.name: map-design
items.cost: Free (MIT). Bundled data is public domain. No API keys
items.works_with: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode and other agents that read Agent Skills
items.short: Your coding agent makes accurate maps, from choropleths to OpenStreetMap city posters, as one HTML, SVG and PNG.
items.what: The skill ships real boundary data, an offline gazetteer and a renderer. Your agent writes a short JSON spec and runs one command, and the renderer draws the map with real borders, coastlines and coordinates. It makes choropleths, bubble, spike and point maps, routes, flow maps, locator maps and city posters. Every place it matched, and every row it couldn't, is listed in a report.
items.who: Anyone who needs a map for a report, slide or post, or a city poster to print. It doesn't do road routing, terrain shading or your own boundary files yet.
needs: Node.js 20 or newer
Optional: Chrome, Edge, Brave or Chromium for PNG export. Without one you still get HTML and SVG
An internet connection for city posters and the `streets` basemap

steps.title: Or install it as a Claude Code plugin
Or copy the folder
steps.text: Copy `skills/map-design/` into your agent's skills folder, for example `~/.claude/skills/map-design`.

steps.title: Ask for a map
steps.text: Ask the way you would ask a designer. The agent writes a spec, runs the CLI, looks at the PNG, fixes what it sees and hands you the files.

steps.title: Or run the CLI yourself
steps.text: From the cloned repo folder. `poster` writes its files to the folder you run it in.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Make a poster of Lisbon in azulejo blue.

watch: Posters download OpenStreetMap vector tiles from OpenFreeMap's free service, which has no uptime guarantee, with the public Overpass API as a fallback.
Raster basemap providers have their own access, cache and export terms, and some need a key. Keep the generated attribution visible.
Borders follow Natural Earth's de facto view, which does not match every government's official position.
The built-in country statistics are Natural Earth's 2019 estimates. For current figures, give the agent a source.
The skill is about 9 MB, mostly bundled open data.

items.name: duo-start
items.works_with: Claude Code as a plugin. Cursor, Codex, Copilot, Gemini CLI and others through the skills CLI
items.short: The starting point for getting an iOS app ready for iPhone Duo: it checks your app, runs a first pass and picks the next Duology skill.
items.what: duo-start is the entry skill of Duology, a pack of 30 skills for Apple's foldable iPhone Duo. It works out whether the app is SwiftUI or UIKit, new or existing, and which SDK it builds with. Then it builds with Xcode 27.1, runs `duo-lint`, checks the app open and closed on the iPhone Duo simulator, writes a short report and routes each problem to one skill.
items.who: iOS developers with a native SwiftUI or UIKit app who want it to work on iPhone Duo. Flutter, React Native and Capacitor apps aren't covered. The skill points those to another repo.
needs: A Mac with Apple silicon
Xcode 27.1 (27A9275 or later) and the iPhone Duo simulator on iOS 27.1
Python, for `duo-lint`
A coding agent that loads AI skills

steps.title: Or install for other agents
steps.text: The CLI finds your agent and installs every skill. Add `--skill <name>` to install one.

steps.title: Check your setup
steps.text: Restart Claude Code first. It checks macOS, Xcode 27.1, the simulator runtime, the iPhone Duo simulator and Python, and changes nothing on its own. On other agents, ask for it in plain words.

steps.title: Ask your agent
steps.text: Ask it to get your app ready for iPhone Duo. duo-start reports what it found before it fixes anything.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Make my app work well on iPhone Duo. Start with an audit, fix what it finds, then run it on the Duo simulator.

watch: It builds through `DEVELOPER_DIR` pointing at Xcode 27.1 and never runs `sudo` or `xcode-select -s`, so your Mac's default Xcode stays the same.
The simulator has no pose command. You click the pose buttons in Device Hub yourself, unless you give the app that runs your agent Accessibility permission.
Exporting Apple's App Resizability skill changes your setup, so the skill asks before it does it.
Everything so far is checked on the simulator only. Checks on a real iPhone Duo and published test results are planned before v1.0.
The first simulator launch with Xcode 27.1 can take several minutes.
